Filter Differential Pressure: Clean vs Dirty Values, Change Out Setpoints, DP Gauges, Switches and Transmitters, Flow Correction and Troubleshooting

A pressure gauge on each side of a filter tells you more about its health than any calendar. Here you will learn what the numbers mean, when to change the element and how flow rate can fool your reading.

Clean vs Dirty dP Change Out Setpoint DP Gauge, Switch, Transmitter Flow Correction Troubleshooting Table

Filter differential pressure is the pressure lost across a filter element, and it rises as dirt builds up. Learn typical clean and change out values, instruments, installation, alarm logic and a flow correction calculator.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn filter differential pressure, how to measure it and how to use it to decide when a filter element needs changing.

What Is Filter Differential Pressure?

Filter differential pressure is the difference between the pressure at the filter inlet and the pressure at its outlet, and it shows how much resistance the element adds to the flow. It starts low with a clean element and rises steadily as particles load the media, so it is the main signal used to decide when to clean or replace a filter.

Quick Answer
  • dP = inlet pressure minus outlet pressure across the filter
  • Clean water cartridges often start near 1 to 3 psi
  • Change out is set by the element maker, such as 2.2 bar for some process cartridges
  • dP falls when flow falls, so compare readings at the same flow
  • Measured with a dP gauge, dP switch or dP transmitter

Filters and strainers both trap solids, but a filter usually removes much finer particles, as explained in our page on the difference between a strainer and a filter. Because the media is finer, filter differential pressure rises faster and needs closer watching.

Solberg Manufacturing shows this gauge across a vacuum inlet filter so operators can read element loading at a glance. The same idea applies to liquid cartridges, bag filters, lube oil filters and air intake filters.

Advertisement

What Is a Normal Differential Pressure for a Filter?

There is no single normal number, because clean pressure drop depends on media grade, element area, fluid viscosity and flow. Boshart notes that a new water cartridge typically shows a drop of about 1 to 3 psi while water is flowing.

Filter TypeClean dP (Typical)Change Out GuideSource
Water cartridge1 to 3 psi5 to 7 psi riseBoshart
Process cartridge housingLow, record at start2.2 barFiltration Group
Vacuum inlet filterRecord at start15 to 20 inH₂O riseSolberg
Any filterBaseline at known flowMaker value or bypass limitElement datasheet

The table shows why you should always write down the clean value at a known flow on the day the element is fitted. That baseline is the reference for every later filter differential pressure reading.

Do You Know?

Solberg recommends changing its inlet filter elements when pressure drop reaches about 15 to 20 inches of water column above the initial value. It also suggests replacing elements after about 8000 hours even if that limit has not been reached.

When Should a Filter Be Changed Based on Differential Pressure?

The best change out point is the value given by the element or housing maker, because they know the collapse and bypass limits of their design. Filtration Group states in its PiP K10 cartridge housing manual that the element should be replaced when a differential pressure of 2.2 bar is reached.

Boshart suggests a change when pressure drop rises about 5 to 7 psi above the clean baseline for water cartridges. Some users change earlier at a 4 to 5 psi rise to save pumping energy, so the setpoint is partly an economic choice.

Clean ElementRecord baseline dP and flow on day one
Loading PhasedP rises slowly as dirt builds a cake
WarningAlarm at about 75 to 80 % of change out value
Change OutReplace at maker limit or fixed time
Never ExceedAbove collapse rating the element can burst or bypass
Quick Tip

Set the warning alarm well below the change out limit so maintenance has time to get a spare element. A warning at about 75 to 80 % of the limit is a common plant practice, not a rule from any standard.

Never let the element run far past its rated limit to save cost. Solberg shows an element that collapsed after exceeding its maximum differential pressure, and a collapsed element passes dirt straight to the equipment it was meant to protect.

Instruments Used for Filter Differential Pressure

dP Gauge

Local dial reading of the pressure difference, often with a coloured change zone.

Best for: Local checks on skids and cartridge housings
Local
Pop Up Indicator

Spring loaded button that pops out at a fixed dP, usually reset by hand.

Best for: Hydraulic and lube oil filters
Visual
dP Switch

Contact changes state at a set dP and sends an alarm to the PLC or panel.

Best for: Simple alarm and duplex changeover
Alarm
dP Transmitter

4 to 20 mA or HART signal of the real dP value for trending in the DCS.

Best for: Critical filters and predictive maintenance
Trend

A differential pressure gauge is the cheapest way to read filter differential pressure locally. For an alarm, a differential pressure switch closes or opens a contact at the setpoint.

Where trending matters, a dP transmitter sends the actual value to the control system. Two separate gauge pressure transmitters can be used, but subtracting two large readings to get a small difference adds error, as shown in static vs differential pressure.

dP Switch
  • Low cost and simple wiring
  • Direct alarm without configuration
  • Good for duplex filter changeover
  • No trend, only a yes or no state
dP Transmitter
  • Continuous value for trending and prediction
  • Several alarms from one signal in the DCS
  • Can apply flow correction in logic
  • Higher cost and needs loop power
Do You Know?

Filtration Group warns that during cold starts the indicator on its cartridge housing may give a warning signal. The visual indicator should only be reset after the fluid reaches operating temperature, and the element changed if the signal returns.

Effect of Flow on Filter Differential Pressure

Pressure drop across a filter depends on flow as well as dirt, so a half loaded element at high flow can show the same reading as a heavily loaded one at low flow. Parker Velcon built its FDPM module for aviation fuel filters under ATA 103 to calculate a corrected dP from measured dP, actual flow and rated flow.

In turbulent flow, pressure drop rises roughly with the square of flow, the same law used in square root extraction for dP flow. Through fine clean media at low velocity the flow is closer to laminar and dP is nearer to linear with flow, so the exponent lies between 1 and 2.

dP corrected = dP measured × (Q rated ÷ Q actual)ⁿ
n = 2 for turbulent, n ≈ 1 for laminar flow
% of limit = dP corrected ÷ limit × 100
Solved example
dP measured = 0.6 bar at Q actual = 30 m³/h
Q rated = 40 m³/h, n = 2, limit = 1.0 bar
dP corrected = 0.6 × (40 ÷ 30)² = 1.067 bar
% of limit = 106.7 %, change the element

At reduced flow the filter differential pressure gauge showed only 0.6 bar, which looks healthy. Corrected to rated flow, the same element is already past its limit, which is why flow correction matters on filters that run at changing loads.

Flow Corrected Filter dP Calculator
Result
Corrected dP 1.067 bar, 106.7 % of change out limit, change element

If your gauges read in psi or inches of water, convert first with a pressure unit converter so the limit and the reading share one unit. Our psi to bar calculator is handy for the same job on site.

How Does a Differential Pressure Switch Work on a Filter?

The high side of the switch connects upstream of the filter and the low side connects downstream. When the pressure difference pushes the diaphragm past the spring setting, a microswitch changes state and the panel shows a filter choked alarm.

Set the switch on rising filter differential pressure at the warning value and check its reset point. The gap between trip and reset is the deadband, which our article on pressure switch setpoint and deadband explains in detail.

1
Check Ratings
Static pressure rating must exceed line pressure, not only the dP range.
2
Fit a Manifold
Use a 3 or 5 valve manifold so the switch can be isolated and equalised.
3
Route Impulse Lines
Keep lines short, sloped and free of trapped gas or liquid.
4
Set and Test
Apply test dP with a calibrator and set the trip on rising pressure.
5
Wire Fail Safe
Use a contact that opens on alarm so a broken wire also alarms.

A valve manifold lets you equalise both sides before isolating the instrument, which protects the sensor from one sided overpressure. Follow the slope rules in impulse line installation so gas pockets do not shift the reading.

Myth: A higher dP always means a dirtier filter.
Fact: dP also rises with flow and viscosity, so compare readings at similar flow and temperature.
Myth: A sudden drop in dP means the filter is clean.
Fact: A sudden drop often means the element has ruptured or the bypass has opened.
Myth: Any dP gauge can go on any filter.
Fact: The gauge must handle full line static pressure on both ports, not just its dP range.
Myth: The element can run until flow stops.
Fact: Past its collapse rating the element can fail and release dirt downstream.

Filter dP Alarm Logic in a PLC or DCS

With a transmitter, the control system can raise a warning alarm, a change out alarm and a high high alarm from one filter differential pressure signal. On duplex filters the high alarm can also prompt the operator to switch to the standby housing.

  • Warning alarm at 75 to 80 % of change out value
  • Change out alarm at the element maker limit
  • Low dP alarm to catch a ruptured element or open bypass
  • Alarm delay of a few seconds to ignore pump start surges
  • Flow permissive so alarms are ignored when the line is stopped
  • Log the dP at each element change for life trending

A low alarm is often forgotten, but it is the only warning of a torn element. Trend the value along with flow, and use the reverse osmosis prefilter as a good example, since membrane life depends on those cartridges.

Quick Tip

If the filter differential pressure trend climbs much faster than usual, check upstream for a process upset such as a tank bottom being drawn or a strainer failure. The filter is often reporting a problem that started somewhere else.

Troubleshooting Filter dP Readings

SymptomLikely CauseWhat to Check
dP stuck at zeroEqualiser open, plugged tappingManifold valves, impulse lines
dP falls suddenlyRuptured element, bypass openElement seal and bypass valve
dP high just after changeWrong element grade, air lockPart number, vent housing
Reading drifts with temperatureViscosity change, zero shiftCompare at same temperature
Alarm at every pump startPressure surge, no delayAdd alarm delay or damping

A plugged impulse line can freeze the reading and hide a choked element, so read our guide to plugged impulse line detection if the value never changes. If a transmitter reads a small dP with no flow, check for transmitter zero shift first.

Filter Differential Pressure FAQ

What is differential pressure in a filter?

It is the inlet pressure minus the outlet pressure across the filter element. The value shows how much resistance the element adds to the flow at that moment.

A clean element gives a low reading that rises as dirt builds up. Operators compare the reading with the element maker limit to decide when to change it.

What is a good differential pressure for a filter?

A good reading is close to the clean value you recorded when the element was fitted at a similar flow. Boshart notes that new water cartridges often show about 1 to 3 psi.

The right number depends on media grade, element size, viscosity and flow rate. Always use the datasheet value for your own filter as the reference limit.

At what differential pressure should a filter be changed?

Change the element at the limit given by the element or housing maker. Filtration Group gives 2.2 bar for its PiP K10 cartridge housing as one example.

For water cartridges, Boshart suggests a change after a rise of about 5 to 7 psi above clean. Time limits can apply first in drinking water service, so check both rules.

Why does filter differential pressure drop suddenly?

A sudden fall usually means the element has torn, a seal has failed or a bypass valve has opened. It can also happen when flow through the filter drops sharply.

Check the flow first, then inspect the element and its seals. A low alarm in the control system helps catch this failure before dirt reaches downstream equipment.

Does flow rate affect filter differential pressure?

Yes, pressure drop rises with flow, roughly with the square of flow in turbulent conditions. At low velocity through fine media it is closer to a straight line relation.

That is why readings should be compared at a similar flow. You can also correct the measured value to rated flow before comparing it with the limit.

Can I use two pressure gauges instead of a dP gauge?

Yes, you can subtract the outlet gauge reading from the inlet gauge reading. This works for rough checks when the pressure drop is large compared with gauge accuracy.

For a small drop at high line pressure, the error of two gauges can be bigger than the value itself. A single dP gauge or transmitter gives a much better reading.

What We Learn Today

  • Filter differential pressure is inlet minus outlet pressure, starts low with a clean element and rises as particles load the media over time.
  • Change elements at the maker limit, set a warning alarm below it and add a low alarm to catch torn elements or an open bypass.
  • Pressure drop changes with flow, so compare readings at similar flow or correct them to rated flow with an exponent between one and two.
